questions.question: Which of the following statements about the GO (G zero phase) phase of the cell cycle is most accurate?

options.text: DNA synthesis occurs rapidly in cells present in the GO phase.
It is the phase where cell division is initiated in cancerous cells.
It is a temporary quiescent stage where cells exit the cell cycle.
Cells in GO actively prepare for DNA replication.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It is a temporary quiescent stage where cells exit the cell cycle.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The GO phase (G zero phase) represents a state of **cell cycle arrest**, where cells exit the active cycle and stop dividing.
 
• Cells in the GO phase are in a **non-proliferative or quiescent state**, often performing specialized functions depending on the cell type.
 
• This phase is **temporary or permanent**, depending on the cell type and environmental conditions.
 
• Examples of cells in permanent GO phase include **neurons and skeletal muscle cells**, which do not divide after differentiation.
 
• GO phase is crucial for **maintaining cellular homeostasis** and protecting against uncontrolled cell division.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cell Cycle Phases:**

 
 
• The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, G2 phases) and mitotic phase (M phase).
 
• GO phase is not part of the active cycle and is considered a resting state.
 
 
 
• **Quiescence vs Senescence:**
 
 
• Quiescence refers to reversible cell cycle arrest (GO phase).
 
• Senescence is an irreversible state of cell cycle arrest caused by damage or aging.
 
 
 
• **Role in Cancer:**
 
 
• Cancerous cells often evade GO phase, leading to uncontrolled division and tumor formation.
 
• Targeting the mechanisms regulating GO phase is a focus in cancer therapy research.
 
 
 
• **Cell Types:**
 
 
• Stem cells can exit GO phase to re-enter the cycle and divide.
 
• Terminally differentiated cells like neurons remain in GO phase permanently.

questions.question: India's improvement in the Rule of Law Index is most critically challenged by which factor?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Slow judicial delivery**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Slow judicial delivery** is one of the most critical issues affecting India's Rule of Law Index ranking.
 
• India's judicial system is burdened with a massive backlog of cases—over 4.5 crore cases were pending in courts as of 2023, according to the National Judicial Data Grid.
 
• The average time to resolve cases in lower courts is several years, while higher courts may take decades to deliver final judgments.
 
• The delay leads to a lack of trust in the justice system, undermining the effectiveness of the Rule of Law in ensuring accountability and fairness.
 
• Factors contributing to slow judicial delivery include insufficient judicial workforce, underfunded courts, procedural complexities, and lack of technological integration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rule of Law Index**

 
 
• The Rule of Law Index is published by the World Justice Project (WJP) and measures how the rule of law is experienced and perceived globally.
 
• The index evaluates factors such as constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, and access to justice.
 
• India ranked 77th out of 140 countries in the 2022 Rule of Law Index.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Backlog in India**
 
 
• As of 2023, over 4.5 crore cases were pending, with nearly 90,000 cases in the Supreme Court alone.
 
• The Law Commission of India has repeatedly recommended increasing the number of judges to address the backlog.
 
 
 
• **National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG)**
 
 
• An online platform that provides real-time data on pending and disposed cases in Indian courts.
 
• It aims to promote transparency and enable better management of case workloads.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Reforms**
 
 
• Proposed reforms include hiring more judges, adopting Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms, and leveraging technology for e-courts.
 
• The E-Courts project is being implemented under the Digital India program to ensure faster and more transparent justice delivery.

questions.question: Which instrument is commonly used in Carnatic classical music?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mridangam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Mridangam** is a percussion instrument widely used in Carnatic classical music, which originated in South India.
 
• It is a double-sided drum, where each side produces different tones, contributing to the rhythmic complexity of Carnatic music.
 
• The Mridangam is often referred to as the "King of Percussion" in Carnatic music due to its prominence in rhythm accompaniment.
 
• Traditionally, it is made from jackfruit wood, and its drumheads are constructed using layers of leather and black paste for tonal resonance.
 
• It serves as the primary rhythm instrument in Carnatic music concerts, often accompanying vocalists and instrumentalists.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Carnatic Music:**

 
 
• Carnatic music is a system of classical music associated with South India, characterized by its intricate melodies and complex rhythmic patterns.
 
• It is based on a system of ragas (melodic frameworks) and talas (rhythmic cycles).
 
• The Mridangam is an essential instrument in Carnatic ensembles, along with the veena, violin, and ghatam.
 
 
 
• **Construction of Mridangam:**
 
 
• The cylindrical body is traditionally made from hollowed jackfruit wood.
 
• The drumheads are crafted using multiple layers of leather, and the black paste (siyahi) in the center helps fine-tune the pitch.
 
 
 
• **Role in Performances:**
 
 
• The Mridangam player provides rhythmic accompaniment, enhancing the overall structure and dynamics of the performance.
 
• It is also used in solo performances, where its intricate rhythmic variations are showcased.
 
 
 
• **Other Instruments in Carnatic Music:**
 
 
• Other commonly used instruments include the violin, veena, flute, and ghatam.
 
• These instruments complement the Mridangam in creating a cohesive musical experience.

questions.question: What trend is reflected by increasing share of urban people in non-manual tertiary occupations?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Emerging service economy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The increasing share of urban people in non-manual tertiary occupations reflects the growth of the **service economy**, where industries like IT, finance, education, and healthcare dominate.
 
• This trend is indicative of a shift from traditional agriculture and manufacturing to a more **knowledge-based economy**.
 
• Urban centers act as hubs for **economic opportunities**, attracting talent for service-oriented roles that require specialized skills and education.
 
• Such a shift has been observed in rapidly urbanizing nations, where the **tertiary sector contributes significantly** to GDP and employment.
 
• The emerging service economy is characterized by increased demand for professional, managerial, and technical roles in cities, driven by globalization and advancements in technology.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Service Economy:**

 
 
• The service economy refers to an economic system where the **majority of economic output and employment** comes from the service sector, rather than agriculture or manufacturing.
 
• Examples include industries like IT, education, healthcare, tourism, and financial services.
 
 
 
• **Urbanization and Economic Shift:**
 
 
• Urbanization leads to the **concentration of infrastructure** and human resources, fostering the growth of service-based industries.
 
• It creates a demand for diverse services in urban centers, such as retail, transport, and education.
 
 
 
• **Role of Technology:**
 
 
• Technological advancements, such as automation and digitalization, have accelerated the transition to a service economy.
 
• IT and telecommunication have enabled remote and global service delivery, expanding economic opportunities.
 
 
 
• **Globalization:**
 
 
• Globalization has connected markets worldwide, boosting the demand for services like IT, finance, and consultancy in urban centers.
 
• It has also facilitated the outsourcing of service-based roles to developing nations.

questions.question: Which region has become the new epicenter of global terrorism, according to the GTI (Global Terrorism Index) 2024?

options.text: Central Sahel region of sub-Saharan Africa

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Central Sahel region of sub-Saharan Africa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Central Sahel region** of sub-Saharan Africa has been identified as the new epicenter of global terrorism, according to the **Global Terrorism Index (GTI) 2024**.
 
• This region includes countries such as **Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger**, which are experiencing a significant rise in terrorist activity.
 
• Jihadist groups such as **Islamic State (IS) affiliates** and al-Qaeda-linked groups are active in this area, causing instability and violence.
 
• Factors contributing to terrorism in the Central Sahel include **weak governance, poverty, ethnic tensions, and competition over natural resources**.
 
• The number of deaths caused by terrorism in this region has surpassed those in the Middle East and North Africa, highlighting its growing significance in global security dynamics.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Global Terrorism Index (GTI):**

 
 
• The GTI is an annual report published by the Institute for Economics and Peace (IEP) that measures the impact of terrorism worldwide.
 
• It uses metrics such as the number of incidents, fatalities, injuries, and property damage to rank countries and regions.
 
 
 
• **Key Terrorist Groups in the Sahel:**
 
 
• **Jama’at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM):** An al-Qaeda-affiliated group active in the Sahel.
 
• **Islamic State in the Greater Sahara (ISGS):** An affiliate of ISIS causing significant instability in the region.
 
 
 
• **Drivers of Terrorism in the Sahel:**
 
 
• Political instability and lack of governance in countries like Mali and Burkina Faso.
 
• Socioeconomic challenges such as poverty and unemployment.
 
• Competition for scarce resources like water and arable land.
 
 
 
• **Regional and International Responses:**
 
 
• Efforts such as the **G5 Sahel joint force**, a regional security initiative, aim to combat terrorism.
 
• International support from organizations like the United Nations and countries like France is critical for counter-terrorism operations.

questions.question: Which high-altitude observatory in India is known for hosting an optical-infrared telescope used for space observation in Ladakh?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hanle Indian Astronomical Observatory**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Hanle Indian Astronomical Observatory is situated at **Hanle in the Union Territory of Ladakh**, India.
 
• It is managed by the **Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA)**, Bengaluru.
 
• The observatory hosts a 2.01-meter Himalayan Chandra Telescope (HCT), which is an advanced **optical-infrared telescope**.
 
• Hanle is one of the highest observatories in the world, located at an altitude of approximately **4,500 meters (14,764 feet)** above sea level.
 
• The site is ideal for astronomical observations due to **clear skies for most of the year** and minimal light pollution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Himalayan Chandra Telescope (HCT):**

 
 
• The HCT is a 2.01-meter telescope equipped with **state-of-the-art instruments** for optical and infrared astronomy.
 
• It is used for studying **stellar objects, galaxies, and other celestial phenomena**.
 
• The telescope is remotely operated from the IIA's CREST campus in Bengaluru.
 
 
 
• **High-Altitude Observatories:**
 
 
• Such observatories are situated at high altitudes to minimize **atmospheric distortion** caused by Earth's dense lower atmosphere.
 
• Examples include the **Mauna Kea Observatories** in Hawaii and the **Very Large Telescope (VLT)** in Chile.
 
 
 
• **Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA):**
 
 
• The IIA is an autonomous research institute under the Department of Science and Technology, Government of India.
 
• It plays a key role in India's **astronomical research and development**.
 
 
 
• **Dark Sky Reserves:**
 
 
• Hanle is being developed as a **Dark Sky Reserve** to promote scientific research and eco-tourism.
 
• Dark Sky Reserves are areas with minimal light pollution, ideal for stargazing and astronomical studies.

questions.question: Which type of galaxy has no regular shape and is rich in gas and dust?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Irregular Galaxy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• An **Irregular Galaxy** is a type of galaxy that lacks a defined shape or structure and does not fall into the categories of elliptical, spiral, or lenticular galaxies.
 
• These galaxies are rich in **gas and dust**, which makes them active regions for star formation.
 
• Irregular galaxies are often influenced by gravitational interactions, such as collisions or close encounters with other galaxies, leading to their distorted appearance.
 
• Examples of irregular galaxies include the **Large Magellanic Cloud** and **Small Magellanic Cloud**, which are satellite galaxies of the Milky Way.
 
• They tend to be smaller than spiral and elliptical galaxies and can house young, hot stars due to ongoing star formation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Galaxy Classification:**

 
 
• Galaxies are broadly classified into four types based on their shape: **Spiral, Elliptical, Lenticular, and Irregular.**
 
• Spiral galaxies have a flat, rotating disk with arms, while elliptical galaxies are round or oval with little gas and dust.
 
• Lenticular galaxies act as a transition between spiral and elliptical galaxies, featuring a disk but no spiral arms.
 
 
 
• **Star Formation in Irregular Galaxies:**
 
 
• The high concentration of gas and dust in irregular galaxies enables the formation of new stars.
 
• These galaxies often host young and massive stars, which emit bright ultraviolet light.
 
 
 
• **Gravitational Interactions:**
 
 
• Irregular galaxies are frequently distorted due to gravitational forces from nearby galaxies.
 
• Such interactions can trigger bursts of star formation and alter the galaxy's shape over time.
 
 
 
• **Large and Small Magellanic Clouds:**
 
 
• The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are the most well-known examples of irregular galaxies.
 
• They are visible from the Southern Hemisphere and are located relatively close to the Milky Way.

questions.question: Consider the emphasis placed on the public sector in India's industrial development strategy between 1947 and 1990. What was a key rationale behind giving the public sector a dominant role during this period?

options.text: There was a lack of demand for industrial goods in the domestic market, necessitating government intervention.
Public sector industries were inherently more efficient than private sector ones.
The private sector had sufficient capital and technological expertise to drive industrialization in all key sectors.
The public sector was seen as a tool for achieving social goals, promoting balanced regional development, and controlling strategic industries.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The public sector was seen as a tool for achieving social goals, promoting balanced regional development, and controlling strategic industries.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Post-independence, India adopted a planned economic model that emphasized state control over key sectors to achieve equitable growth and reduce socio-economic disparities.
 
• The public sector was assigned a dominant role to address strategic industries like defense, infrastructure, and energy, ensuring national security and self-reliance.
 
• Balanced regional development was a priority; public sector enterprises were established in economically backward areas to create employment and uplift local economies.
 
• The government aimed to use public sector industries to fulfill social welfare goals, such as reducing income inequality and providing essential goods and services at affordable prices.
 
• The private sector was relatively weak in terms of capital, technology, and organizational capacity, necessitating a strong public sector presence during this period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956:**

 
 
• The policy classified industries into three categories, with the first group reserved exclusively for the public sector.
 
• It emphasized state ownership and control over industries of national importance, such as defense, railways, and atomic energy.
 
 
 
• **Five-Year Plans:**
 
 
• The first Five-Year Plan (1951-1956) focused on agricultural development, while subsequent plans prioritized industrialization with public sector investments.
 
• The Second Five-Year Plan (1956-1961) was heavily influenced by the Mahalanobis model, which advocated for public sector-led growth in heavy industries.
 
 
 
• **Strategic Industries:**
 
 
• Strategic industries like steel, coal, and petroleum were nationalized to ensure stability, security, and self-reliance in critical sectors.
 
• These industries were considered vital for national defense and economic sovereignty.
 
 
 
• **Public Sector Contribution:**
 
 
• By the 1980s, public sector enterprises accounted for a significant share of industrial output, employment, and exports.
 
• They played a pivotal role in building infrastructure like roads, railways, and power generation facilities.
 
 
 
• **Challenges Faced:**
 
 
• Despite its contributions, the public sector faced issues like inefficiency, overstaffing, and lack of competitiveness, leading to economic reforms in 1991.
 
• The reforms introduced privatization and liberalization to address these challenges and encourage private sector participation.

questions.question: In what way did fiscal discipline reforms affect center-state financial relations post-1991?

options.text: States had to adhere to fiscal targets
Increased state autonomy in tax policy

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**States had to adhere to fiscal targets**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Post-1991 fiscal reforms, states were mandated to adhere to **fiscal deficit reduction targets** to qualify for central funds and grants.
 
• The introduction of the **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act** encouraged states to adopt disciplined fiscal practices.
 
• States were required to implement measures such as **limiting borrowings**, improving tax collection efficiency, and reducing non-productive expenditures.
 
• The central government provided incentives for states achieving fiscal targets, such as **debt relief packages** and additional financial assistance.
 
• Such reforms aimed at strengthening macroeconomic stability and ensuring better utilization of resources at both the central and state levels.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act**

 
 
• The FRBM Act was enacted in 2003 to ensure fiscal discipline and reduce fiscal deficits.
 
• It set targets for reducing the fiscal deficit and revenue deficit as a percentage of GDP.
 
• States were encouraged to adopt their own FRBM legislation in alignment with the central framework.
 
 
 
• **Debt Relief Measures for States**
 
 
• Post-reforms, states achieving fiscal targets were provided with debt restructuring and relief packages by the central government.
 
• These measures helped in reducing the financial burden on states and incentivized fiscal discipline.
 
 
 
• **Macro-Fiscal Stability**
 
 
• Fiscal discipline reforms contributed to improving macroeconomic stability by reducing the fiscal deficit and ensuring sustainable growth.
 
• Efficient allocation of resources between the center and states became a key priority.
 
 
 
• **Tax Sharing Post-Reforms**
 
 
• The 1991 reforms emphasized rationalizing tax structures to improve revenue collection.
 
• While states retained autonomy in certain tax domains, the central government introduced mechanisms for equitable tax sharing.

questions.question: Which of the following agro-climatic and soil conditions is most suitable for the cultivation of wheat?

options.text: Arid crop; temperature above 40°C; sandy loam soil
ubtropical crop; high humidity; laterite soil
Temperate crop; winter temp 10-15°C, summer 21-26°C; clay loam soil

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Temperate crop; winter temp 10-15ºC, summer 21-26ºC; clay loam soil**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Wheat** is a temperate crop that thrives in regions with moderate temperatures during its growing period.
 
• Optimal temperature for wheat growth is **10-15ºC during winter** (for germination and vegetative growth) and **21-26ºC during summer** (during maturation).
 
• Wheat requires **clay loam soil** with good water retention capacity and adequate drainage for proper root development.
 
• Regions with **low humidity** and a well-distributed rainfall pattern are ideal for wheat cultivation.
 
• India’s major wheat-growing regions include Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh, which have suitable agro-climatic conditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Wheat Cultivation:**

 
 
• Wheat is a rabi crop (winter crop) sown in October-November and harvested in March-April.
 
• It is the **second most important cereal crop in India** after rice.
 
• Major wheat varieties grown in India include HD 2967, PBW 343, and WH 1105.
 
• India is the **second-largest producer of wheat in the world** after China.
 
 
 
• **Soil Requirements:**
 
 
• Clay loam soil is preferred as it retains moisture and provides essential nutrients.
 
• Soil pH for wheat cultivation should ideally be between **6.0 and 7.5**.
 
• Proper soil aeration and drainage prevent root diseases and ensure healthy crop growth.
 
 
 
• **Climatic Requirements:**
 
 
• Wheat is a temperate crop requiring a cool climate during germination and growth stages.
 
• Excessive heat (>30ºC) or frost can significantly affect wheat yield.
 
• Rainfall between **50-75 cm** during the growing period is ideal.
 
 
 
• **Global Wheat Production:**
 
 
• Globally, wheat is cultivated in temperate regions like the USA, Canada, Russia, and Europe.
 
• Countries with advanced irrigation systems and soil management practices yield higher wheat productivity.

questions.question: According to Lenz's Law, what determines the direction of an induced current in a conductor?

options.text: It continuously reduces the applied magnetic flux,
It always enhances the existing magnetic field.
It flows to oppose the variation in magnetic flux causing it.
It is proportional to the strength of the magnetic field.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It flows to oppose the variation in magnetic flux causing it**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Lenz's Law states that the direction of the induced current in a conductor is such that it **opposes the change in magnetic flux** that caused it.
 
• The law is based on the **principle of conservation of energy**, ensuring that the induced current doesn't create energy out of nothing.
 
• This opposition is achieved by the induced current generating a magnetic field that counters the change in the external magnetic flux.
 
• Lenz's Law can be mathematically expressed as part of Faraday's Law: **E = -dΦ/dt**, where the negative sign indicates opposition to the change.
 
• It plays a critical role in understanding electromagnetic induction and is widely applied in devices like electric generators, transformers, and inductors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction:**

 
 
• It states that a change in magnetic flux through a circuit induces an electromotive force (EMF) in the circuit.
 
• The induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of the magnetic flux.
 
• Faraday's Law forms the foundation for Lenz's Law.
 
 
 
• **Conservation of Energy:**
 
 
• Lenz's Law ensures that the induced current's opposition prevents the creation of perpetual motion, adhering to energy conservation.
 
• The opposing magnetic field consumes energy equivalent to the work done to change the magnetic flux.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Lenz's Law:**
 
 
• Lenz's Law is crucial in designing **electric generators**, where mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy.
 
• It is also applied in **transformers** to regulate voltage levels and prevent energy losses.
 
• Induction cooktops utilize Lenz's Law to generate heat efficiently.
 
 
 
• **Key Terminology:**
 
 
• **Magnetic Flux (Φ):** The measure of the total magnetic field passing through a surface.
 
• **Electromotive Force (EMF):** The voltage generated by changing magnetic flux.
 
• **Induced Current:** The current generated due to electromagnetic induction.

questions.question: What led to the decline of Timurid power in the second half of the 15th century?

options.text: Economic decline due to maritime trade shifts

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Internal wars due to partitioning**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The decline of Timurid power in the second half of the 15th century was significantly influenced by **internal conflicts among the Timurid princes**.
 
• After the death of Timur (Tamerlane) in 1405, the empire was divided among his successors, leading to **fragmented governance**.
 
• This partitioning resulted in **widespread internal wars** as various princes fought to expand their territories and consolidate power.
 
• The weakening caused by these internal struggles allowed external forces, such as the **Uzbeks**, to exploit the situation and rise as a dominant power in Central Asia.
 
• Timurid rulers also faced challenges in maintaining effective central authority due to their reliance on **nomadic tribal alliances**, which further destabilized the empire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Timurid Empire:**

 
 
• Founded by Timur (Tamerlane) in the late 14th century, the Timurid Empire spanned parts of Central Asia, the Middle East, and South Asia.
 
• Timur aimed to restore the Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan and ruled through a combination of military conquests and alliances.
 
 
 
• **Partitioning of the Empire:**
 
 
• Timur's empire was divided among his sons and grandsons, leading to decentralized rule and frequent conflicts.

• **Role of the Uzbeks:**

• The fall of Herat in 1507 marked the definitive end of Timurid dominance in the region.
 
 
 
• **Cultural Contributions:**
 
 
• Despite political decline, the Timurids made significant cultural contributions, particularly in art, architecture, and Persian literature.
 
• Herat, under the patronage of rulers like Sultan Husayn Bayqara, became a renowned center of Timurid culture.

questions.question: Which planet has the longest day in the solar system?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Venus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Venus** has the longest day in the solar system, with one day on Venus lasting approximately 243 Earth days.
 
• The rotation of Venus is **retrograde**, meaning it rotates in the opposite direction to most other planets, including Earth.
 
• Its slow rotation is due to gravitational interactions and tidal forces between Venus and the Sun.
 
• A day on Venus is longer than its year, which lasts about 225 Earth days.
 
• Venus' dense atmosphere and slow rotation contribute to extreme surface temperatures and atmospheric conditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Retrograde Rotation:**

 
 
• Retrograde rotation occurs when a planet spins in the opposite direction to its orbital motion around the Sun.
 
• Venus and Uranus are the only planets in the solar system with retrograde rotation.
 
 
 
• **Atmosphere of Venus:**
 
 
• Venus has a thick atmosphere composed mostly of carbon dioxide, with clouds of sulfuric acid.
 
• The atmospheric pressure on Venus is about 92 times that of Earth, making it the most extreme among terrestrial planets.
 
 
 
• **Temperature on Venus:**
 
 
• The surface temperature of Venus can reach up to 465°C (869°F), hotter than Mercury, despite being farther from the Sun.
 
• This is due to a runaway greenhouse effect caused by its dense atmosphere.
 
 
 
• **Orbital Characteristics:**
 
 
• Venus is the second planet from the Sun and is sometimes referred to as Earth's "sister planet" due to its similar size and composition.
 
• Its orbit is nearly circular, with an eccentricity of less than 0.01.

questions.question: What is one of the major future impacts of ISRO's Aditya-L1 mission that studies the Sun's chromosphere and corona?

options.text: Enhanced rainfall prediction in monsoon regions
Improved space weather forecasting to protect satellites and power systems

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Improved space weather forecasting to protect satellites and power systems**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• ISRO's Aditya-L1 mission focuses on studying the Sun's chromosphere, corona, and solar magnetic field, which are crucial for understanding space weather dynamics.
 
• One of the mission's primary objectives is to enhance **space weather forecasting capabilities**, helping mitigate disruptions to satellites, communication systems, and power grids.
 
• By monitoring solar activity, including coronal mass ejections and solar flares, Aditya-L1 will provide real-time data to predict geomagnetic storms.
 
• Improved space weather forecasting is essential for ensuring the safety of astronauts, satellites, and infrastructure critical to modern life, such as GPS and power systems.
 
• Aditya-L1's positioning at the Lagrange Point 1 (L1) provides a continuous view of the Sun, enabling uninterrupted observations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Space Weather:**

 
 
• Space weather refers to conditions on the Sun and in the solar wind that can influence Earth's magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere.
 
• Major components include solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and high-speed solar wind streams.
 
• Geomagnetic storms caused by space weather can affect satellite functionality, disrupt GPS signals, and cause power outages.
 
 
 
• **Lagrange Point 1 (L1):**
 
 
• L1 is a stable point located between the Earth and the Sun where gravitational forces balance out, allowing a spacecraft to stay fixed relative to both celestial bodies.
 
• This position provides uninterrupted views of the Sun, making it ideal for solar observation missions like Aditya-L1.
 
 
 
• **Aditya-L1 Instruments:**
 
 
• The spacecraft is equipped with seven payloads, including the Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC) and Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT).
 
• These instruments are designed to study various aspects of the Sun, such as its magnetic field, solar winds, and energy transfer mechanisms.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Earth:**
 
 
• Improved understanding of solar activity can protect critical infrastructure like power grids, aviation routes, and communication networks.
 
• Such insights can also aid in planning space missions and ensuring the safety of astronauts in space.

questions.question:
Read the following statements about Trade Policy Reform:

Statement I: Trade policy reform in India involved removing quantitative restrictions on imports and exports.

Statement II: Trade policy reform increased import licensing to support domestic manufacturers.

options.text: Both statements I and II are correct
Both statements I and II are incorrect

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 4: Only Statement I is correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Statement I:** Trade policy reform in India involved removing quantitative restrictions on imports and exports. This was a key feature of the economic liberalization initiated in 1991.
 
• Quantitative restrictions were removed to promote **global trade integration** and allow free-market principles to operate.
 
• India reduced import tariffs, liberalized export policies, and removed licensing requirements for many goods and services during this reform phase.
 
• **Statement II:** Incorrect—Import licensing was reduced, not increased, to foster competition and allow easier access to foreign goods.
 
• The reforms aimed to make India a competitive player in the global market by reducing bureaucratic hurdles and encouraging foreign investments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Economic Liberalization of 1991:**

 
 
• India faced a severe balance of payments crisis in the early 1990s, prompting the government to adopt economic liberalization measures.
 
• The reforms were spearheaded by then Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh under PM P.V. Narasimha Rao’s leadership.
 
• Key elements included trade liberalization, industrial deregulation, fiscal consolidation, and financial sector reforms.
 
 
 
• **Quantitative Restrictions:**
 
 
• These are non-tariff barriers that limit the quantity of goods that can be imported or exported.
 
• India’s removal of these restrictions was aligned with WTO guidelines to promote fair trade practices.
 
 
 
• **Import Licensing:**
 
 
• Before 1991, many imported goods required government licensing, which restricted access to foreign products.
 
• The reforms reduced licensing requirements to encourage competition and provide consumers access to high-quality goods.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Trade Policy Reform:**
 
 
• India witnessed a sharp increase in foreign trade, with exports and imports growing significantly.
 
• Foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows increased, boosting industrial and economic growth.
 
• The reforms led to greater integration of the Indian economy with global markets.

questions.question: Which of the following reflects the 'what to produce' decision in economics?

options.text: Choosing between capital and consumer goods
Increasing taxes to raise government revenue

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Choosing between capital and consumer goods**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 'what to produce' decision in economics refers to the allocation of resources to produce goods and services that meet societal needs and preferences.
 
• Choosing between capital goods (used for production) and consumer goods (used for direct consumption) reflects this decision, as it impacts economic growth and consumption patterns.
 
• This decision is influenced by factors such as resource availability, market demand, and government policies.
 
• Economists consider the opportunity cost of producing one type of good over another to optimize societal welfare.
 
• In planned economies, the government plays a key role in determining 'what to produce,' while in market economies, this is largely determined by consumer demand and producer supply.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Capital Goods:** These are goods used in the production of other goods, such as machinery, tools, and buildings. They contribute to long-term economic growth.
 
• **Consumer Goods:** These are goods intended for immediate consumption by individuals, such as food, clothing, and electronics.
 
• **Opportunity Cost:** The cost of foregone alternatives when choosing one option over another, critical in economic decision-making.
 
• **Planned Economy:** An economic system where the government decides resource allocation, production, and distribution of goods and services.
 
• **Market Economy:** An economic system where decisions regarding production and consumption are guided by market forces such as supply and demand.

questions.question: Which economic consequence of migration is generally considered a challenge for the destination regions in India, particularly concerning unskilled rural migrants?

• Destination regions may experience **overburdened urban infrastructure** due to the influx of unskilled migrants, leading to challenges such as housing shortages and inadequate sanitation.
 
• Employers in the informal sector often exploit migrant workers by offering **low wages** and poor working conditions.

questions.question: Under Section 25(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, what may the Court do when a person is convicted in one trial for multiple offences?

options.text: Can impose only one punishment for all the offences, regardless of their nature
Must give the harshest punishment only and remit other punishments altogether
Shall suspend all sentences unless directed by a higher court in the same trial
May impose punishments to run either concurrently or consecutively as appropriate

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**May impose punishments to run either concurrently or consecutively as appropriate**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Section 25(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 provides discretion to the Court when multiple offences are tried in a single trial.
 
• The Court can decide whether the punishments for multiple offences should run **concurrently (at the same time)** or **consecutively (one after another)**, based on the circumstances of the case.
 
• This ensures that the sentencing is proportional and tailored to the nature and gravity of the offences committed.
 
• The provision seeks to balance the principles of justice and deterrence while preventing excessive or overlapping punishments.
 
• The discretion under this section aligns with practices in criminal jurisprudence to uphold fairness in sentencing.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Concurrent Sentences:**

 
 
• When sentences run concurrently, the convict serves time for multiple offences simultaneously.
 
• This method is typically applied for related or less severe offences.
 
 
 
• **Consecutive Sentences:**
 
 
• When sentences run consecutively, the convict serves time for one offence after completing the sentence for another.
 
• This method is usually applied for unrelated or more severe offences.
 
 
 
• **Principles of Sentencing:**
 
 
• Sentencing aims to achieve deterrence, retribution, rehabilitation, and societal protection.
 
• The proportionality principle ensures that the punishment fits the gravity of the crime.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Discretion:**
 
 
• Judges have discretion under the law to interpret and apply sentencing provisions based on case facts.
 
• Discretion is guided by precedents, legal principles, and legislative intent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Residuary powers refer to the authority to legislate on matters not enumerated in the Union List, State List, or Concurrent List of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Under Article 248 of the Indian Constitution, Parliament has exclusive power to legislate on residuary subjects.
 
• This provision is supported by Entry 97 of the Union List in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution.
 
• Examples of residuary subjects include matters related to cyberspace, atomic energy, and other emerging technologies not envisioned at the time of drafting the Constitution.
 
• Unlike in federal systems like the USA, where residuary powers are given to the states, in India, these powers are vested in the central authority to ensure a strong and unified center.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• It contains three lists: Union List, State List, and Concurrent List, which define the distribution of powers between the Centre and States.
 
• Union List: Contains subjects of national importance (e.g., defense, foreign affairs).
 
• State List: Contains subjects of local or state-level importance (e.g., police, public health).
 
• Concurrent List: Contains subjects where both the Centre and States can legislate (e.g., education, marriage).
 
 
 
• **Article 248 of the Constitution:**
 
 
• It grants Parliament exclusive power to legislate on matters not enumerated in any of the three Lists.
 
• This ensures that emerging or unforeseen areas of legislation are uniformly governed across the country.
 
 
 
• **Residuary Powers in Federal Systems:**
 
 
• In India, residuary powers are vested in the Centre, unlike the USA, where they are given to the states.
 
• This reflects the quasi-federal nature of the Indian Constitution, prioritizing a strong central government.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Interpretation:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court of India has upheld the exclusive power of Parliament over residuary matters in several landmark cases.
 
• It ensures that no legislative vacuum exists in matters that may arise due to technological or societal advancements.

questions.question:
Arrange the following Fundamental Rights in the order of their appearance in the Constitution:

1. Right to Freedom

2. Right to Equality

3. Right to Freedom of Religion

4. Right against Exploitation
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2) 2-1-4-3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, from Articles 12 to 35.
 
• The sequence of Fundamental Rights is as follows:
 
 
• Right to Equality (Articles 14-18)
 
• Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22)
 
• Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24)
 
• Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28)
 
 
 
• Option 2 correctly arranges these rights in the order of their appearance in the Constitution: 2-1-4-3.
 
• These rights collectively aim to protect individual liberties and uphold equality, non-discrimination, and freedom of conscience.
 
• The Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning individuals can approach the judiciary if their rights are violated.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Right to Equality:**

 
 
• Prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth (Article 15).
 
• Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws (Article 14).
 
• Abolishes untouchability and titles except for military or academic distinctions (Articles 17-18).
 
 
 
• **Right to Freedom:**
 
 
• Includes freedom of speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession (Article 19).
 
• Protects individuals from arbitrary detention (Articles 20-22).
 
 
 
• **Right against Exploitation:**
 
 
• Prohibits human trafficking, forced labor, and exploitation of children (Articles 23-24).
 
 
 
• **Right to Freedom of Religion:**
 
 
• Ensures freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion (Article 25).
 
• Prohibits the imposition of religious taxes and ensures the secular character of educational institutions (Articles 27-28).

questions.question:
Read the following and choose the correct option:

Assertion (A): Sound waves travel faster in steel than in air at the same temperature.

Reason (R): The particles in solids (like steel) are more closely packed and experience stronger intermolecular forces compared to particles in gases (like air), allowing vibrations to be transmitted more efficiently and rapidly.

options.text: A is false but R is true..
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Sound waves travel faster in steel than in air** because the density and elastic properties of steel allow efficient transmission of vibrations.
 
• Steel, being a solid, has particles that are **closely packed**, enabling faster propagation of sound waves.
 
• In contrast, air, being a gas, has particles that are far apart, leading to slower transmission of sound waves.
 
• **Intermolecular forces in solids** like steel are stronger, which helps in quicker transfer of energy between particles.
 
• The speed of sound in steel is approximately **5,960 m/s**, while in air, it is around **343 m/s** at room temperature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sound Wave Propagation:**

 
 
• Sound waves are mechanical waves that require a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel.
 
• The speed of sound depends on the medium's density and elasticity.
 
 
 
• **Elastic Modulus and Density:**
 
 
• The elastic modulus (stiffness of the material) is higher in steel, contributing to faster sound propagation.
 
• Density affects sound speed inversely: lower density generally leads to slower sound speed in gases compared to solids.
 
 
 
• **Intermolecular Forces:**
 
 
• Stronger intermolecular forces in solids ensure quicker energy transfer between particles.
 
• In gases, weaker forces and larger intermolecular distances result in slower sound transmission.
 
 
 
• **Speed of Sound in Different Media:**
 
 
• Steel: ~5,960 m/s
 
• Water: ~1,480 m/s
 
• Air: ~343 m/s
 
• These values vary with temperature and material composition.
 
 
 
• **Temperature Effects:**
 
 
• In gases, the speed of sound increases with temperature due to increased kinetic energy of particles.
 
• In solids and liquids, temperature changes have a lesser impact compared to gases.

questions.question: Who set up a Dayanand Anglo Vedic school in Lahore?

• He established the Dayanand Anglo Vedic (DAV) School in Lahore in 1886 as part of his efforts to promote education and social reform.

• Promoted education, especially for women, and emphasized Sanskrit as a medium of learning.

questions.question: Which of the following was a major criticism of the industrial policy followed in India during 1950-1990?

options.text: Creation of a protected market leading to inefficiency and lack of innovation.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Creation of a protected market leading to inefficiency and lack of innovation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The industrial policy during 1950-1990 in India promoted a **protectionist approach**, heavily relying on import substitution and limited competition from foreign markets.
 
• Excessive **state control and regulation**, often termed as the "License Raj," stifled private sector growth and innovation.
 
• The policy fostered a **protected market**, allowing domestic industries to operate without competition, leading to inefficiency, poor-quality products, and lack of technological advancements.
 
• The lack of exposure to international markets and competition **hindered the development of globally competitive industries** in India during this period.
 
• The restrictive industrial policies resulted in a **slow pace of economic growth** and inadequate industrial diversification in the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **License Raj**

 
 
• A system of elaborate licenses, permits, and regulations implemented in India between 1947 and 1990 to control industries.
 
• It required businesses to obtain multiple licenses and clearances, which led to bureaucratic delays and corruption.
 
 
 
• **Import Substitution Industrialization (ISI)**
 
 
• An economic policy adopted by India to reduce foreign dependency by promoting domestic production of industrial goods.
 
• While it aimed to build self-reliance, it resulted in inefficiencies due to lack of competition and innovation.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956**
 
 
• The policy classified industries into three categories: those exclusively owned by the state, those progressively state-controlled, and those open to private sector participation.
 
• It emphasized the role of the public sector in achieving economic and social goals.
 
 
 
• **Liberalization in 1991**
 
 
• The economic reforms of 1991 marked the end of the License Raj and introduced measures to liberalize, privatize, and globalize the Indian economy.
 
• This reform era dismantled trade barriers, reduced state control, and encouraged foreign investments, spurring industrial growth and innovation.

questions.question: The Jog Falls in Karnataka is formed from which river?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sharavathi River**__.

__
 
• Jog Falls is formed by the **Sharavathi River**, which flows through the state of Karnataka.
 
• It is one of the highest plunge waterfalls in India, with a height of approximately **253 meters (830 feet).**
 
• Located in the **Shimoga district** of Karnataka, Jog Falls is a major tourist attraction and known for its breathtaking beauty.
 
• The waterfall is divided into four distinct cascades: **Raja, Rani, Roarer, and Rocket**.
 
• Jog Falls is primarily fed by the monsoon rains and the Sharavathi River, making it a seasonal waterfall with peak flow during the rainy season.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sharavathi River:**

 
 
• Originates in the Western Ghats, near Ambuthirtha in Karnataka.
 
• Flows westward and eventually drains into the Arabian Sea.
 
• Sharavathi River is dammed at the **Linganamakki Dam**, which is a major source of hydroelectric power in Karnataka.
 
 
 
• **Jog Falls:**
 
 
• Unlike other waterfalls, Jog Falls is a **plunge waterfall**, meaning the water drops vertically without touching the rock face.
 
• During peak monsoon, the falls are at their most majestic, attracting thousands of tourists.
 
 
 
• **Hydroelectric Power:**
 
 
• The Sharavathi River is a significant source of **hydroelectric power generation** in Karnataka.
 
• The Linganamakki Dam has a capacity of generating approximately **1,035 MW of electricity**.
 
 
 
• **Tourism in Karnataka:**
 
 
• Jog Falls is part of Karnataka's rich natural heritage and is one of the state's primary eco-tourism destinations.
 
• Shimoga district, where Jog Falls is located, is also known for lush greenery and diverse flora and fauna.

questions.question: What kind of approach does the Happiness Index encourage in governance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Citizen-centric**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Happiness Index promotes governance that prioritizes the **well-being, satisfaction, and happiness of citizens** over purely economic or resource-driven goals.
 
• This approach ensures that policies and initiatives are designed to address the **physical, mental, and emotional needs of the population**.
 
• It emphasizes the importance of **inclusive growth, social equity, and environmental sustainability** in decision-making.
 
• Governments adopting a citizen-centric approach focus on **education, healthcare, income equality, and environmental quality** as key determinants of happiness.
 
• The Happiness Index is aligned with the idea that governance should aim to **enhance the overall quality of life** rather than prioritizing mere economic indicators like GDP.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Happiness Index**

 
 
• The Happiness Index, also known as the World Happiness Report, is an annual publication by the United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network.
 
• It ranks countries based on factors like GDP per capita, social support, life expectancy, freedom, generosity, and corruption perception.
 
• The report uses data from surveys conducted by organizations like Gallup and relies on the Cantril Ladder method to measure happiness.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Citizen-Centric Governance**
 
 
• Bhutan's Gross National Happiness (GNH) framework prioritizes cultural preservation, environmental conservation, and citizen well-being.
 
• Scandinavian countries, such as Finland and Denmark, consistently rank high on the Happiness Index due to their focus on social welfare, healthcare, and education.
 
 
 
• **Legalistic vs. Citizen-Centric Approach**
 
 
• A legalistic approach emphasizes adherence to laws and regulations, often prioritizing institutional frameworks over individual needs.
 
• A citizen-centric approach focuses on creating policies and systems that directly address the needs and aspirations of citizens.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Citizen-Centric Governance**
 
 
• Enhances trust between the government and its citizens.
 
• Improves overall satisfaction and productivity within the population.
 
• Encourages participatory governance and inclusive decision-making.

questions.question: Who was the Home Minister in the first cabinet of free India?
questions.solution:

__
 
• **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** served as the first Home Minister of independent India from 15 August 1947 to 15 December 1950.
 
• He was also the first **Deputy Prime Minister** of India under the leadership of Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.
 
• As Home Minister, Sardar Patel played a pivotal role in the **integration of princely states** into the Indian Union post-independence.
 
• He is often referred to as the **"Iron Man of India"** for his strong leadership and efforts to unify the country.
 
• Sardar Patel was instrumental in handling the internal security and administrative challenges of a newly independent India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Role of the Home Minister:**

 
 
• The Home Minister is responsible for maintaining **internal security**, law and order, and the implementation of the Constitution within the country.
 
• Other key responsibilities include overseeing the operations of central armed police forces, disaster management, and border management.
 
 
 
• **Integration of Princely States:**
 
 
• At the time of independence, India had over 560 princely states that had to choose between joining India, Pakistan, or remaining independent.
 
• Sardar Patel, with the help of V.P. Menon, successfully integrated most princely states into the Indian Union through negotiation and diplomacy.
 
• Notable examples include the integration of Hyderabad, Junagadh, and Kashmir.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Role:**
 
 
• Sardar Patel was a key member of the **Constituent Assembly** and contributed to the drafting of India’s Constitution.
 
• He emphasized the importance of a strong central government to maintain unity and stability in the country.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Sardar Patel's contributions to Indian unity are commemorated with the **Statue of Unity**, the world’s tallest statue, located in Gujarat.

questions.question: Which act replaces the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)** is a proposed law aimed at replacing the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973, as part of the Indian government’s initiative to modernize criminal laws.
 
• It was introduced in **August 2023** in the Lok Sabha by the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, along with two other bills for comprehensive legal reforms.
 
• The BNSS is designed to ensure a more **efficient, citizen-centric, and technology-driven criminal justice system** in India.
 
• The bill focuses on reducing delays in investigation and trial processes, enhancing transparency, and strengthening mechanisms for protecting citizens' rights.
 
• Provisions in the BNSS include **time-bound investigations**, electronic submissions, and the use of modern technology to improve the overall efficacy of the criminal justice system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS):**

 
 
• Proposed to replace the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860.
 
• Aims to modernize penal provisions and incorporate stricter laws for crimes such as mob lynching and sexual offenses.
 
• Focuses on victim-centric justice and timely prosecution.
 
 
 
• **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA):**
 
 
• Proposed to replace the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
 
• Introduces new provisions for **digital evidence** and admissibility of electronic records.
 
• Emphasizes simplifying evidence laws to make them more relevant to contemporary issues.
 
 
 
• **Key Objectives of Criminal Law Reforms:**
 
 
• The reforms aim to provide **speedy justice** and ensure that justice is accessible to every citizen.
 
• They focus on enhancing the use of technology in investigations and trials.
 
• Ensuring that laws are victim-centric, especially in cases involving women, children, and marginalized groups.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The CrPC, IPC, and Indian Evidence Act were introduced during British rule and have undergone several amendments since independence.
 
• The need for reforms has been discussed in various commissions, including the **Malimath Committee Report** of 2003.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the goal of stem cell therapy in modern medicine?

options.text: To provide genetic immunity against viruses
To prevent blood clotting in arteries
To replace or regenerate damaged tissues or organs

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To replace or regenerate damaged tissues or organs**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Stem cell therapy** aims to replace or regenerate damaged tissues or organs, offering a potential cure for various debilitating diseases.
 
• Stem cells are unique because they have the ability to differentiate into various specialized cell types, such as muscle, nerve, or blood cells.
 
• This therapy is being extensively researched for conditions like **spinal cord injuries, diabetes, Parkinson’s disease, and heart disease**.
 
• Stem cells can be derived from **embryonic stem cells, adult stem cells, or induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)**, providing multiple avenues for treatment.
 
• The goal is not just repair but also to restore normal function to damaged tissues or organs, which traditional medicine often cannot achieve.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Stem Cells:**

 
 
• These are undifferentiated cells capable of dividing and renewing themselves over long periods.
 
• They have the ability to differentiate into specialized cell types.
 
• Two main types: **embryonic stem cells** (pluripotent) and **adult stem cells** (multipotent).
 
 
 
• **Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs):**
 
 
• iPSCs are adult cells reprogrammed to behave like embryonic stem cells.
 
• They eliminate ethical concerns associated with using embryonic stem cells.
 
• iPSCs are widely used in regenerative medicine and disease modeling.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Stem Cell Therapy:**
 
 
• Bone marrow transplants for blood disorders like leukemia.
 
• Potential treatments for neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s.
 
• Regeneration of damaged organs such as the heart, liver, or kidneys.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Stem Cell Therapy:**
 
 
• Ethical concerns regarding embryonic stem cells.
 
• High costs and complex procedures.
 
• Risks such as immune rejection or tumor formation.

 Column B: Capital

The correct answer is __**1) 1-a, 2-b, 3-d, 4-c**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Vatsa Mahajanapada had its capital at **Kaushambi**, which was an important trade and political center in ancient India.
 
• Magadha’s capital was **Rajagriha (modern-day Rajgir)**, which was a significant hub for political and religious activities during the Mahajanapada period.
 
• The Kuru Mahajanapada had its capital at **Indraprastha**, which is associated with the modern-day Delhi region.
 
• The capital of Avanti Mahajanapada was **Ujjayini**, known for its cultural and religious importance in ancient times.
 
• These capitals were significant centers of administration, trade, and culture during the time of the Mahajanapadas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mahajanapadas:**

 
 
• The term "Mahajanapada" refers to the sixteen large states or kingdoms that existed in ancient India during the 6th century BCE.
 
• These states were spread across the Indo-Gangetic plains and were the precursors to later empires such as the Maurya and Gupta dynasties.
 
• The Mahajanapadas were classified into monarchies and republics, with governance structures varying between them.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Capitals:**
 
 
• Capitals like Rajagriha, Kaushambi, Ujjayini, and Indraprastha were strategic centers for trade, culture, and governance.
 
• These cities were often fortified and served as seats of power for their respective rulers.
 
• Capitals also played a key role in the spread of religion, especially Buddhism and Jainism during this period.
 
 
 
• **Geographical Spread:**
 
 
• The Mahajanapadas were located in modern-day regions of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and parts of Pakistan.
 
• This geographical distribution highlights the diversity and cultural richness of ancient India.
 
 
 
• **Religious and Cultural Significance:**
 
 
• Many of the Mahajanapadas, such as Magadha, played a vital role in the development and spread of Buddhism and Jainism.
 
• These regions were home to several important religious councils and gatherings.
